intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, tells you what to remember and warns you where people slip. Work the examples in pencil, answer the recall questions without looking, and keep a notebook beside you for your own observations.

sections.title: Why Observation Matters
sections.big_idea: Observation records **what people actually do**, so it catches the say-do gap, the unasked question and the routine nobody mentions.
in_plain_words: Most development evidence is what people tell us. Surveys, interviews and records each fail in a different way, and observation fails in its own: the observer is present and changes the scene. The argument is for using more than one method. Observation is the one that can surface something nobody thought to ask about.

The say-do gap is the distance between reported and observed behaviour. It opens because memory reconstructs, norms shape answers and habits sit below awareness. **Read the gap as information about norms and practice, never as lying.** Watch at every stage of a project, and most of all during implementation.

left.title: What people say
items: Fails when reporting differs from doing

right.title: What people do
items: Shows the routine and the unasked
Fails when the observer changes the scene

key_terms.meaning: Systematically watching, listening and recording behaviour in the field.
The distance between reported and observed behaviour.
Something real that nobody would report as a problem.
Something absent from the survey instrument.
A habit so ordinary that respondents forget to mention it.
Feel for a place built by being there; a guide that is not evidence in itself.

worked_example.title: Size a say-do gap
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a mother says the family always washes hands before eating. You watch 20 meals over a week and see handwashing at 7 of them.
steps: Meals watched with no handwashing: 20 − 7 = 13.
Share of meals with handwashing: 7 ÷ 20 = 35%.
Reported practice is 'always', so the gap is large.
Two readings: practice is lower than reported, and the family endorses handwashing as the right thing.
Record both, because the pair tells you which is which.
worked_example.answer: Handwashing at 35% of meals against a report of 'always'; the gap is the finding.

mistakes: Treating the gap as dishonesty. People usually report the practice they endorse, which is real information about norms.
Assuming observation is more truthful than a survey. It is wrong about different things.
Using observation to get prevalence. It cannot, and a survey can.
Leaving observation until evaluation, when a half-day in month three would have caught a delivery problem.

recall.q: How does the deck define observation?
recall.a: Systematically watching, listening to and recording behaviour, interactions and settings in the field to understand what happens as well as what people say happens.

recall.q: Name two reasons the say-do gap opens.
recall.a: Any two of: memory reconstructs, norms shape what is sayable, habits run below awareness, the question implies a right answer.

recall.q: Which kinds of thing does a survey miss?
recall.a: The unspoken, the unmeasured, the contextual and the routine.

recall.q: What can observation not tell you?
recall.a: Prevalence. For that you need a survey.

recall.q: Which project stage is the most under-used for observation?
recall.a: Implementation.

sections.title: Types of Observation
sections.big_idea: Every observation sits on **three axes**: role, structure and disclosure. Decide each one on purpose, and state them in your methods.
in_plain_words: Role runs from complete participant to complete observer, with two positions between. More participation buys depth and trust, and less buys distance and comparability. Structure runs from open notebook to checklist, and the usual sequence is unstructured first, then structured. Disclosure is overt or covert, and overt is the default.

The three axes are independent, and most studies drift into non-participant, semi-structured and overt without anyone choosing. **Match the type to the question before the fieldwork is scheduled**, because the type sets the time required. Some private or sensitive questions are better left to other methods.

diagram.root: Every observation sits on three axes
diagram.caption: state all three in the methods section

key_terms.meaning: The observer takes part in the life of the setting.
The observer stays apart, which makes records more comparable.
Counting pre-defined things with a checklist or timer.
People know they are watched and have consented.
People do not know; consent is impossible.
Behaviour changes when people know they are watched.

worked_example.title: Match the question to a type
worked_example.setup: Three questions arrive from a programme manager. Use the deck's table to lean toward a design for each.
steps: 'Why does uptake differ here?' Lean participant, then follow with interviews.
'How do sites compare?' Lean non-participant and structured.
'Does the attendance record match reality?' Use brief non-participant, structured observation.
A fourth question concerns something private or sensitive: probably not an observation question at all.
In every case state role, structure and disclosure in the methods.
worked_example.answer: Participant then interviews; non-participant structured; brief structured check; and decline the sensitive one.

mistakes: Letting role, structure and disclosure be decided by default instead of by design.
Drifting along the participant spectrum without recording when and why.
Building a checklist before open observation has shown what belongs on it.
Choosing covert observation when prolonged overt engagement would reduce the observer effect.

recall.q: What are the three axes that define an observation?
recall.a: Role, structure and disclosure.

recall.q: What does Gold's continuum order?
recall.a: Observer roles from complete participant to complete observer.

recall.q: Which sequence do most good studies follow on structure?
recall.a: Unstructured first, then structured.

recall.q: Why is overt the ethical default?
recall.a: It gives consent; covert denies people the chance to consent and carries serious risk.

recall.q: What does the deck say about sensitive questions?
recall.a: Some should not be answered by watching, and choosing observation because it is available is a risk.

sections.title: What to Observe
sections.big_idea: Watch with a **structure**: Spradley's nine dimensions, a grand tour first, then a narrowing funnel, and always ask who is absent.
in_plain_words: A busy site overwhelms the eye and tires you in an hour. Spradley's nine dimensions give you a lens: space, actors, activities, objects, acts, events, time, goals and feelings. Begin with a grand tour that maps the whole setting, then narrow to a mini-tour, moving from descriptive to focused to selective observation.

A framework also blinds. A programme's own logframe will find out whether it did what it said and never what else is happening. **Hold your lens firmly enough to be systematic and loosely enough to be surprised.** Draw a sketch map in every session, and keep a column for things that do not fit.

spokes.label: Actors
spokes.sub: who is here, who is not

diagram.caption: Spradley's nine dimensions, grouped in six

key_terms.meaning: Nine features present in any social situation.
A broad sweep of the whole setting before zooming in.
A close look at one corner or activity.
A quick map of doorways, seating and movement.
Taking in everything, noting all nine dimensions.
Counting specific, well-defined behaviours.

worked_example.title: Read an anganwadi and plan sessions
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's anganwadi table. Meal service comes first and weighing follows. Two mothers are present with 18 children.
steps: Ask the Actors question: which mothers are present, and where are the others?
Ask the Time question: do mothers stay for the weighing that follows the meal?
If they leave after eating, growth monitoring silently fails.
Plan sessions you can sustain: three observations of 40 minutes.
3 × 40 = 120 minutes of watching across the sessions.
worked_example.answer: The sequence of meal then weighing is the lead to follow; 120 minutes in three sessions keeps the quality high.

mistakes: Recording whatever catches the eye because no framework was chosen.
Starting at the selective phase and counting categories you assumed.
Ignoring absence, the finding frameworks built on what is present never prompt.
Sitting through an unfocused half-day when shorter sessions with breaks would give better notes.

recall.q: Name three of Spradley's nine dimensions.
recall.a: Any three of: space, actors, activities, objects, acts, events, time, goals, feelings.

recall.q: What is the grand tour for?
recall.a: Taking in the whole setting before narrowing, so you learn what to focus on.

recall.q: Why is 'who is not here' the most productive question?
recall.a: Absence is a finding, and no framework built from what is present will prompt it.

recall.q: What are the three phases of the funnel?
recall.a: Descriptive, focused, selective.

recall.q: Why keep a column for things that don't fit?
recall.a: That column is often where the insight hides.

sections.title: Field Notes
sections.big_idea: If it is not written down, it did not happen: **write the same day, keep description apart from interpretation**, and record exact words.
in_plain_words: Memory decays and reshapes itself to fit your expectations. A week later you hold a story shaped around your conclusion, and it feels vivid. So take brief jottings in the field and write full expanded notes the same day, budgeting about an hour of writing per hour observed.

Keep layers apart: descriptive, reflective, analytic and personal. Describe low-inference behaviour first. Thick description records context and meaning, so a reader can check your reading. **Quote the phrase you did not follow, in the speaker's language.** The notebook is the instrument, so protect it and back it up.

events.what: Everything, but you cannot write it all
A story shaped to fit your conclusion

diagram.caption: what survives, and why the same-day rule has no exceptions

key_terms.meaning: Quick keywords, quotes and sketches taken in the field.
The full scene written up the same day.
Observable detail anyone could have recorded.
An action recorded with its context and meaning.
Marker for an observer comment, kept apart from fact.
Exact words in the speaker's language, in quotation marks.

worked_example.title: Turn a judgement into a description
worked_example.setup: Illustrative classroom note: 'The class was disengaged.' In the room, 30 children were present; you saw 11 with heads down and 4 writing.
steps: The judgement 'disengaged' cannot be checked, so replace it with what you saw.
Write: eleven of thirty had heads down; four were writing.
Share with heads down: 11 ÷ 30 = 36.7%.
Children unaccounted for: 30 − 11 − 4 = 15.
Note what the other 15 were doing, and mark any reading as [OC].
worked_example.answer: A checkable description (11 of 30 heads down, 4 writing) with 15 children still to describe.

mistakes: Writing up 'later'. Memory reorganises around your conclusion.
Recording a label such as 'hostile' instead of the folded arms and the silence.
Paraphrasing a striking quote and losing the speaker's own terms.
Organising notes by theme at the start, so analysis has already been applied.

recall.q: What is the golden rule of fieldnotes?
recall.a: Write up the same day.

recall.q: How much writing time should you budget?
recall.a: Roughly an hour of writing for each hour observed, more at the start.

recall.q: What is the difference between descriptive and reflective notes?
recall.a: Descriptive notes record what you saw and heard; reflective notes record what you think it means.

recall.q: What does thick description add?
recall.a: The context and meaning that let a reader judge whether your interpretation is right.

recall.q: What should every note header contain?
recall.a: Date, time, place and who was present.

sections.title: Structured Observation Tools
sections.big_idea: Structure trades richness for reliability: use it **once you know what matters**, and make every definition work for two observers.
in_plain_words: Checklists record present or absent, rating scales record degree, time sampling takes snapshots at intervals, and event sampling records every occurrence. An observation guide sits between a notebook and a checklist. Pick the tool by whether you need to discover, compare or track.

A tool is only as good as its definitions. Operationalise every behaviour you count, anchor every point on a scale with something observable, and test inter-observer agreement. **Pilot in the real setting**, then fix the items two observers read differently. Report the interval, the definition and the number of sessions.

diagram.caption: from the most open instrument to the most fixed

key_terms.meaning: A list of defined things recorded as present or absent.
A concrete description of what a scale point looks like.
Observing at set intervals to show what is typical.
Recording every occurrence of a defined event.
An exact rule any observer applies the same way.
How often two observers record the same result.

worked_example.title: Plan a time-sampling tally
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a 40-minute lesson is observed with a snapshot every 5 minutes, and children are counted as on-task using a written definition. On six snapshots most of the class was on-task.
steps: Number of snapshots: 40 ÷ 5 = 8.
On-task snapshots: 6 of 8.
Share of snapshots on-task: 6 ÷ 8 = 75%.
Eight snapshots is a small sample for a claim about a lesson.
One lesson is not the teacher, so plan more sessions.
worked_example.answer: Eight snapshots with 75% on-task; report the interval, definition and sessions, and add more lessons.

mistakes: Writing 'toilet functional' with no definition, so each observer decides for themselves.
Using time sampling on a rare event and reading the zeros as meaningful.
Leaving scale points unanchored, which produces everyone choosing the middle.
Never measuring agreement, so nobody knows if the counts mean anything.

recall.q: When should you choose structure?
recall.a: When you know what matters, need to compare sites, have several observers or will track change.

recall.q: What is the difference between time and event sampling?
recall.a: Time sampling records at set intervals; event sampling records every occurrence.

recall.q: What does anchoring a scale point mean?
recall.a: Describing it with something observable, such as roughly half the class following the activity.

recall.q: What does low overall inter-observer agreement tell you?
recall.a: The instrument is not ready.

recall.q: Why pilot in the real setting?
recall.a: A tool that works at a desk can fail in a room with eighteen children.

sections.title: Sensemaking: Notes to Patterns
sections.big_idea: Sensemaking is analysis: **notes become codes, codes become themes, themes become insight**, with a visible trail of what you discarded.
in_plain_words: After fieldwork you hold a pile. Code the notes with short labels, group similar codes, and build themes that recur and answer your question. Write dated memos throughout, since the best ideas arrive in the field. Themes are constructed, and two competent analysts will build different ones, so transparency matters more than claiming objectivity.

Hunt for the case that does not fit and report what you made of it. Give counts with denominators, such as 9 of 12 sessions. Say saturation only with a stopping rule. **An audit trail written as you go is a record; one rebuilt afterwards is a justification.**

diagram.caption: the coding loop, repeated until the set is stable

key_terms.meaning: A short dated note capturing a hunch, question or link.
A short label tagging a recurring idea in the notes.
A pattern that recurs and answers your question.
An observation that breaks your pattern.
New observation stops yielding new themes.
Codebook, extracts, memos and decisions showing your path.

worked_example.title: Report a count with its denominator
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a workaround code appears in 9 of 12 observed sessions at anganwadis. You did not sample the anganwadis at random.
steps: Convert the count to a share of your sessions: 9 ÷ 12 = 75%.
Write: 'in 9 of 12 observed sessions', which is a fact about your fieldwork.
Do not write '75% of anganwadis', which is a claim about a population you did not sample.
For the other 3 sessions, find out what was different.
Record that you did not observe it in those 3, and write nothing stronger.
worked_example.answer: Report 9 of 12 observed sessions (75% of sessions), with no population percentage.

mistakes: Skipping coding, so the findings are whatever the analyst remembers most vividly.
Presenting themes that mirror the observation guide as if they were discovered.
Smoothing over the anomaly that breaks the pattern.
Claiming saturation with no stopping rule and no test.

recall.q: What are the four steps from pile to insight?
recall.a: Notes, codes, themes, insight.

recall.q: What are the four tests for a theme?
recall.a: Does it recur, answer your question, differ from other themes, and have supporting extracts.

recall.q: Why write memos during fieldwork?
recall.a: The best ideas arrive in the field and then vanish; memos make them a traceable trail.

recall.q: What makes a saturation claim credible?
recall.a: A stated stopping rule, such as three sessions with no new codes.

recall.q: What should an audit trail contain?
recall.a: The codebook, example extracts, how themes were built, decisions that changed and a reflexive journal.

sections.title: Triangulation
sections.big_idea: No single method sees everything: **combine methods, sources and observers**, and treat disagreement as a lead.
in_plain_words: Triangulation borrows from surveying, where two bearings fix a point. Observation shows what people do, interviews what it means to them, and documents and data the scale. Observe first and then interview, so your questions refer to a specific event. Test registers and minutes against the room.

Convergence counts only if sources are independent and could have disagreed. Divergence is information: investigate it and report it. **Pair observers who differ in gender, language or background**, and compare notes before discussing interpretations. Record which method produced which claim.

diagram.caption: Denzin's four types; most people use only method

key_terms.meaning: Using more than one method, source or observer on a question.
Independent sources pointing the same way.
Sources disagreeing, which is itself a finding.
Showing your reading to those observed.
Who you are, and how it shapes what you see.
Errors that differ across sources, which makes agreement informative.

worked_example.title: Read a divergence
worked_example.setup: The attendance sheet says 30 children and you counted 18 in the room on the day you visited.
steps: Size the gap: 30 − 18 = 12 children.
Express the count as a share of the sheet: 18 ÷ 30 = 60%.
Reading one: reporting pressure on the sheet.
Reading two: you came on an atypical day.
Gather more evidence, such as other visits or an interview, before choosing a reading.
worked_example.answer: A gap of 12 children (60% present); two readings stay open until more evidence arrives.

mistakes: Counting two observers from the same organisation as independent confirmation.
Treating divergence as proof that one source is lying.
Adding a second method only at write-up.
Leaving the divergence out of the report because it is harder to write than agreement.

recall.q: What are Denzin's four types of triangulation?
recall.a: Method, source, observer and theory.

recall.q: Why observe before interviewing?
recall.a: It lets you ask about the specific thing you watched and use people's own vocabulary.

recall.q: When is convergence meaningful?
recall.a: When methods are independent, could have disagreed, and the sources have different biases.

recall.q: How should you handle an attendance sheet that disagrees with the room?
recall.a: Treat it as a finding and look for more than one reading.

recall.q: Why pair observers who differ in background?
recall.a: They notice different things, and the difference is data.

sections.title: From Insight to Action
sections.big_idea: An insight is **actionable and non-obvious**; test every finding with 'so what?' and write recommendations with an owner and a date.
in_plain_words: A pattern is not yet an insight, and an insight is not yet a decision. Ask 'so what?' of every finding. An insight changes how you understand the problem and points somewhere. The mechanism, which observation is well placed to supply, turns a fact into an insight.

Recommendations need an owner and feasibility checked with the person who must act. Feed findings back to frontline workers and communities in a usable form, since they can correct your misreading. Do not over-reach: a few sites cannot prove a district claim. **Lead with the insight and the decision it implies.**

diagram.note: a fact that is not both actionable and non-obvious stays a fact

key_terms.meaning: The question that turns a finding into a decision.
A finding that is actionable and non-obvious.
Who should do what, by when, and feasible.
Taking findings back to those observed.
Routine observation with no route to someone who can change things.
Claiming population certainty from a few vivid visits.

worked_example.title: Turn a fact into an insight
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: attendance at an anganwadi is low. Observation shows weighing follows the meal and mothers leave after eating.
steps: The fact: 'attendance is low'. It is not actionable or non-obvious.
The mechanism: mothers leave before the weighing because it runs after the meal.
The insight: moving the weighing session changes the outcome.
The recommendation: shift the weighing session to before the meal, with the supervisor confirming the new time.
Check feasibility with the worker who would run it.
worked_example.answer: Fact to insight to action: move weighing before the meal, owned by the supervisor.

mistakes: Reporting facts as insights, such as 'attendance is low'.
Writing recommendations such as 'improve services' with no owner.
Claiming a district-wide pattern from a handful of sites.
Keeping insights in a report that never returns to the people who generated them.

recall.q: What two properties make a finding an insight?
recall.a: It is actionable and non-obvious.

recall.q: What makes a recommendation usable?
recall.a: It is specific, owned and feasible, with who, what and by when.

recall.q: What does member checking add?
recall.a: A validity check and an ethical courtesy, since workers correct misreadings.

recall.q: What can observation at a few sites carry?
recall.a: A mechanism, a hypothesis and evidence that a practice exists.

recall.q: How should a report open?
recall.a: With the insight and its so-what, with methodology in the annex.

sections.title: Bias & Rigour
sections.big_idea: There is no neutral camera: rigour is **managing and disclosing bias** with named disciplines, and none of them removes it.
in_plain_words: You select what to record, perceive selectively, interpret and change the scene. The observer effect fades with time. Selective attention hides what you expected not to see, and a second observer is the real remedy. Confirmation bias is the most dangerous because it feels like insight.

Going native loses the outsider's view, and reflexivity records your assumptions and reactions as data. Positionality names who you are and how that shapes access. **Combine prolonged engagement, triangulation, disconfirming cases, low-inference notes, an audit trail and peer debriefing**, and report which you used.

diagram.caption: each source of bias with its discipline

key_terms.meaning: People behave differently when they know they are watched.
The eye filters by what you expect and care about.
Noticing and weighting what fits your beliefs.
Identifying with the group and losing distance.
Examining and recording how you shape what you see.
A colleague who was not there challenges your reading.

worked_example.title: Pick the discipline for each bias
worked_example.setup: Four situations arise in the same study. Match each to a discipline from the deck's table.
steps: Staff behave better on your first announced visit: use repeat visits and name the effect.
You keep noticing cases that fit your idea: write expectations beforehand and hunt for disconfirming cases.
You stop questioning how the group does things: arrange peer debriefing and time away.
A funding agency badge changes what people show you: name your positionality in the methods.
Report which disciplines you used, and which you could not.
worked_example.answer: Repeat visits; disconfirming cases; peer debriefing; naming positionality.

mistakes: Claiming neutrality instead of naming the observer's position.
Believing individual effort can fix selective attention, when only a second observer helps.
Treating going native as understanding, since it feels like it from inside.
Writing the reflexive journal at the end, which makes it recollection.

recall.q: What is the observer or Hawthorne effect?
recall.a: People behave differently when they know they are being watched.

recall.q: Why is confirmation bias the most dangerous?
recall.a: It feels like insight, because the pattern gets clearer as you notice confirming cases.

recall.q: What is the remedy for selective attention?
recall.a: A second observer, plus writing expectations down beforehand.

recall.q: What is positionality?
recall.a: Naming how your gender, caste, class, age, language and agency shape what you can see.

recall.q: Which technique does the deck call cheapest and least used?
recall.a: Peer debriefing.

sections.title: Ethics of Observation
sections.big_idea: You are watching real lives: **ethics runs through every minute**, from consent and privacy to what you write and what you give back.
in_plain_words: Observation enters people's routines, often with nothing flowing back. Consent has to be informed, continuous and costless to refuse, and a gatekeeper's permission is not a person's consent. Privacy duties change with the setting, from open public space to a private home. Cameras and recorders need their own consent.

Power shapes consent: a request from an official's companion can feel impossible to refuse. What you write can identify someone in a small village. Covert work needs four conditions at once and independent approval. **Reciprocity means findings returned in a usable form, with a budget line and a date.**

levels.label: Open public space
levels.sub: observe; do not single people out

diagram.caption: duties rise with the expectation of privacy

key_terms.meaning: Knowing who you are, what you record, where it goes and that they may decline.
A person whose permission opens access but does not replace consent.
The observer's literacy, backing and ability to leave.
Naming someone through combined attributes.
What flows back to those observed.
Law covering identifiable digital data, including images.

worked_example.title: Plan consent for a clinic visit
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: the block officer gives you permission to observe a clinic queue and you want to photograph the waiting area.
steps: The clinic is semi-public, so you need institutional permission and individual consent.
The officer's permission opens the door; it is not consent from the woman in the queue.
Ask separately from the official, in her language, and make declining visibly costless.
Photographs need separate explicit consent, and people may say yes to observation and no to the camera.
Decide storage and deletion before fieldwork; DPDP duties apply from 13 May 2027.
worked_example.answer: Get both institutional and individual consent, separate consent for photos, and plan data storage in advance.

mistakes: Treating consent to be observed as consent to be photographed or published.
Describing a person by village, gender, age and role, which identifies them with no name.
Asking for consent in front of the official who arrived with you.
Promising feedback to the community and not delivering it, which damages trust for later observers.

recall.q: Why is a headmaster's permission not a child's consent?
recall.a: Gatekeepers grant access, but the person observed must also agree, and may decline at no cost.

recall.q: What are the four conditions for covert observation?
recall.a: Important knowledge, no other method, minimal harm and independent ethics approval.

recall.q: What extra consent do cameras need?
recall.a: Separate, explicit consent, which is not covered by consent to be observed.

recall.q: How can you protect identity in a small village?
recall.a: Coarsen details, since combinations of attributes identify people, and store notes securely.

recall.q: What is the ethical test of fieldwork?
recall.a: Would the people observed feel fairly treated if they read everything you wrote?

sections.title: Practice & Tools
sections.big_idea: Plan before you go, use one page for notes, and **write up the same day**: the methods are simple and the discipline is scarce.
in_plain_words: Decide before the field: the question, the type, site and timing, the tool, consent and recording. Timing is a sampling decision in disguise, so visit at more than one time of day and day of the week if you want to say what is typical. Use a one-page note template with a sketch map, two columns and follow-ups.

Paper beats apps for jottings, voice memos help you expand notes on the way home, KoboToolbox or ODK handle offline counts, and a spreadsheet or Taguette handles coding. **Tools serve the method.** The common mistakes are all habits, led by writing up later.

diagram.caption: the planning questions, answered before you go

key_terms.meaning: A one-page format with header, map, columns, quotes and follow-ups.
Questions carried to the next session.
Dictating expanded notes on the journey home.
Free offline tools for structured counts.
Free software for coding notes.
The visit slot decides what you can say is typical.

worked_example.title: Plan sessions and writing time
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: you want to say what is typical at an anganwadi. You visit at 3 times of day on 2 days of the week, one hour per visit, and budget an hour of writing per hour observed.
steps: Number of sessions: 3 × 2 = 6.
Hours observed: 6 × 1 = 6.
Hours of writing at one per hour observed: 6 × 1 = 6.
Total time including writing: 6 + 6 = 12 hours.
Also plan a one-page template and a piloted guide.
worked_example.answer: Six sessions and twelve hours including the same-day write-up.

mistakes: Writing up 'later'. Three days on, notes have reorganised around your conclusion.
Observing whenever it was convenient and then calling the findings typical.
Letting the template change between sessions, which makes comparison impossible.
Using coding software for rigour when a spreadsheet would do.

recall.q: What is the single most effective practical habit in the deck?
recall.a: Dictating expanded notes on the journey home.

recall.q: What belongs in a field-note header?
recall.a: Date, time, place, observer and who was present.

recall.q: Name the five takeaways on slide 99.
recall.a: Watch what people do, use a framework, write up the same day, triangulate, observe ethically.

recall.q: What does the deck recommend for a first study?
recall.a: Keep Spradley open and start with Emerson, Fretz and Shaw if you go to the field this month.

recall.q: Why vary the time and day of visits?
recall.a: Observing at one time tells you only about that time.

notes.2: Eleven sections run from why observation matters to practice and tools. Read them in order the first time, because later sections lean on the earlier ones. If you are heading to the field soon, start with sections 4, 10 and 11, then return to the rest.
notes.4: Observation is learning by watching what people do in real settings, and it has its own rigour. The table shows each method failing differently, which is the argument for **using more than one**. Keep the last point in mind: observation can surface what nobody thought to ask about.
notes.5: People say one thing and do another, and the cause is rarely dishonesty. Memory reconstructs, norms shape answers and habits sit below awareness. **The gap is the finding.** 'We always wash hands' tells you about the norm, and watching tells you about practice.
notes.6: The chart is invented, so read it only for its shape: reported handwashing sits well above observed handwashing. **Do not quote the figures.** The warning underneath is the point, since a programme built on self-report alone can chase a behaviour that was never there.
notes.7: A questionnaire returns answers only to questions you already knew to ask. Observation adds four categories: the unspoken, the unmeasured, the contextual and the routine. The routine is richest and hardest to see, so **write down what strikes you in the first week**, before it becomes ordinary.
notes.8: Choose by what the question needs. Surveys count, interviews explain, records show what was written, and observation shows what happened. Each has a blind spot. For prevalence, observation cannot help; for mechanism, a survey cannot. **Triangulation is a design decision** made at the start.
notes.9: Time in the field builds a feel for rhythm, space and tension that data cannot carry, and repeated presence earns candour. Use that tacit understanding to choose your questions and what to watch for, but **do not present it in your findings as though it were evidence**.
notes.10: Use the table to see what observation adds at each project stage. The slide calls implementation the most under-used row: half a day of observation in month three would have found the delivery problem. **Build light observation into supervision** so the programme corrects itself in time.
notes.11: Watching is interpretation, and two observers can record different things. The table pairs each risk with a discipline, such as defined categories or disconfirming cases. None removes the risk; they **make it visible and checkable**. The rest of the deck expands this one table.
notes.13: Fix three choices before you enter the field: role, structure and disclosure. They are independent, and most studies drift into non-participant, semi-structured and overt by default. **Decide each on purpose and state all three in your methods** so a reader can judge your findings.
notes.14: Gold's continuum has four positions, from complete participant to complete observer. More participation buys depth and trust, and less buys distance and a wider view. You will move along it, which is fine if you **record when and why you moved**. Undocumented drift makes a methods section unverifiable.
notes.15: Participant observation gives trust, felt understanding and backstage moments, and costs time, distance and a changed scene. Note-taking is the hard part, since you cannot write through a group meeting. Plan jotted notes and same-day write-up, and **decide beforehand what you will do if you witness something that needs action**.
notes.16: Standing apart gives cleaner, more comparable records across more sites, at the price of meaning and trust. You can time the queue and still not learn why people accept its order. A watcher with a clipboard is **an event in the room** and still alters behaviour.
notes.17: Structured tools count and unstructured notes discover. Follow the slide's sequence: unstructured first to learn what matters, then structured to count it. Many studies invert this because checklists are easier to budget, and they end with **a precise count of categories that turned out not to matter**.
notes.18: Overt is the default: people know and have consented, and you accept some observer effect. Covert denies consent and rarely gets approval. The observer effect fades with time, so **prolonged overt engagement gives you what deception was meant to**. Section 10 sets the bar for covert work.
notes.19: Choose the type from the question, and do it before the calendar is fixed. The table matches questions to leanings. Hold on to the last row: some private or sensitive questions **should not be answered by watching at all**. A design chosen after the schedule is set will be chosen by the schedule.
notes.21: A busy site overwhelms the eye, and watching harder does not help. A framework tells you what to look at, lets patterns build up across sessions and makes observers comparable. Plan sessions you can sustain: **three good forty-minute observations beat one unfocused half-day**.
notes.22: Spradley's nine dimensions are a checklist for any social situation: space, actors, activities, objects, acts, events, time, goals, feelings. Run through all nine before narrowing. The least obvious ones (objects, time, feelings) are where surprises sit. **Always ask who is not here.**
notes.23: Start broad. Walk and map the whole space, note who is present and who is absent, watch a full cycle, and only then narrow to a mini-tour of one corner. Frameworks built from what is present never prompt you to look for absence. **Do the grand tour before you pick a focus.**
notes.24: See the nine dimensions applied at an anganwadi, then read the questions in the second table. The fourth row hides a finding: if weighing follows the meal and mothers leave after eating, **growth monitoring silently fails**. The sequence of activities decides whether a service reaches people.
notes.25: Draw the space, badly and quickly. A sketch map shows doorways, seating, queues and where the worker stands, and space encodes hierarchy. Who sits on the mat and who on the chair is a caste and gender fact **no interview would surface as such**. Keep one in every notebook.
notes.26: Observation funnels over time: descriptive, then focused, then selective. It is a sequence, and you cannot choose one stage alone. Starting selective counts categories you assumed, which **produces confident irrelevance**. Budget time for the descriptive phase, since it looks unproductive and makes the rest valid.
notes.27: Your lens focuses attention and also blinds you. The table shows what each framework helps with and what it hides, and the programme's own logframe is the practitioner's trap. **Keep a column for things that don't fit**, and worry if it stays empty session after session.
notes.29: Notes are the raw data. The table shows memory decaying: by a week later you hold a story shaped to fit your conclusion, and it feels vivid. **Write up the same day, without exception.** Back-to-back sessions with no writing time give worse data than fewer sessions would.
notes.30: Take quick jottings in the field and write the full scene the same day. Jottings are the seed and expanded notes are the crop. Budget **about an hour of writing for each hour observed**. Keep jotting unobtrusive, because visible note-taking changes the behaviour you came to see.
notes.31: Keep what you saw apart from what you think it means. Use a marker such as [OC] for observer comments, in separate columns or colours. The four-layer table adds analytic and personal notes. **Separate layers make your analysis auditable**, for you in months and for any reviewer.
notes.32: Record behaviour and leave your label out. 'Hostile' is a judgement, while 'folded her arms, looked away, answered in one word' is something anyone could have recorded. Labels can be revised and lost observations cannot be recovered, so **describe first and interpret second**.
notes.33: Thick description records an action with its context and meaning, as in Geertz's twitch and wink. The slide's real point is checkability: give the reader enough context to **judge whether your interpretation is right**. If they have no basis to disagree, you have assertion with field notes attached.
notes.34: Write striking speech word for word, in the speaker's language, in quotation marks, with who said it and when. Mark your paraphrases too. **The phrase you did not follow is the one to write down exactly**, because local terms for obligation or shame often carry the finding.
notes.35: Five habits keep notes usable. Head every note with date, time, place and who was present. Write in sequence, record absences, separate quotes from your own thoughts. The header takes ten seconds and has **the best payoff on the list**. Number your pages and never tear any out.
notes.36: In observation you are the instrument and the notebook is its output, so treat it like a calibrated gauge. It is confidential, because field notes identify people, and it holds the only copy. **Photograph or transcribe it each day** and store it securely. Never hand it to the programme you observed.
notes.38: Structure trades richness for reliability. Use it when you know what matters, need to compare sites, have several observers or will track change. It is what makes many observers **poolable**. The prerequisite comes from earlier work: count only what unstructured observation told you matters.
notes.39: A checklist records present or absent. Make every item observable and define judgement words, so 'toilet functional' becomes water present, a door that closes and no storage use. **Anything that needs judgement belongs on an anchored rating scale** instead of a yes or no tick.
notes.40: A rating scale measures degree, but only if every point is anchored with something observable. 'Moderate engagement' is no anchor; 'roughly half the class following the activity' is. Pilot with two observers. **Unanchored scales produce central tendency**, which looks like consensus in the data.
notes.41: Time sampling takes snapshots at set intervals to show what is typical, and event sampling records every occurrence to show how often and in what order. Pick by whether you care about **states or events**. Time sampling a rare event gives zeros that mean nothing.
notes.42: The chart is invented to show the method. Snapshots every five minutes of a 40-minute lesson give eight data points, a small sample for any claim about the lesson. **Report the interval, your definition of on-task and the number of sessions**, or nobody can interpret the tally.
notes.43: An observation guide sits between a free notebook and a checklist: a one-page prompt list with room to describe. It steers without closing off discovery. Write it as questions, since 'Who is served first, and how is that decided?' prompts more than **a bare category such as service order**.
notes.44: Write exactly what counts as on-task or aggressive before you go, and test it. Include edge cases, such as a child looking at another child's book. **Two observers will disagree at the edges**, so a definition that looks obvious in the office needs a field test.
notes.45: Have two observers code the same session independently, then compare. High agreement means the tool is usable, and low agreement on one item means that item's definition needs work. Many field checklists are **never tested this way**, so nobody knows whether the counts mean anything.
notes.46: Pilot every instrument in the real setting. Look for items observers read differently, forms too slow for the session, definitions that fail at the edges and categories that never occur. A checklist that works at a desk can fail in a room with eighteen children. **Pilot first, then fix.**
notes.48: Sensemaking turns notes into codes, codes into patterns, patterns into themes and themes into insight. Each step discards material on purpose, which is what makes it analysis. **Do not skip coding**, or your findings are whatever you remember most vividly. Keep an audit trail of what you set aside.
notes.49: Write short dated memos throughout fieldwork: a hunch, a question, a link between sessions, a change of mind. Memos are the first draft of your findings. **Half a page written when the idea forms** beats a day of analysis months later trying to recover it. Keep them with the notes.
notes.50: Coding tags stretches of notes with short labels so you can gather one idea across every session. That turns twelve observations into a pattern. Follow the four steps. The slide singles out **workaround** as productive: where staff break a rule to deliver, the rule is usually the finding.
notes.51: Themes are built from repeated codes and then tested. Ask whether each recurs, answers your question, differs from the others and has supporting extracts, including ones that complicate it. **Watch for themes that mirror your observation guide**: six prompts giving six themes means the notes were sorted and nobody analysed them.
notes.52: Hunt for the case that does not fit. Ignoring it or explaining it away leaves a tidy pattern that is partly false. Stating the condition it reveals gives a pattern with known limits. **The one anganwadi where the queue works differently** tells you what the others depend on. Report it.
notes.53: Give counts with denominators: 'in 9 of 12 observed sessions' beats 'often'. Write 'we did not observe this' and never 'this does not happen', because **twelve sessions is weak evidence of absence**. A count of sessions describes your fieldwork and says nothing about a population you did not sample.
notes.54: Saturation means new observation stops yielding new themes. It applies to one question at one breadth and to nothing else. Claim it only with a stated stopping rule, such as three sessions with no new codes. **If the fieldwork length was fixed in advance, say so.**
notes.55: Rigour is transparency. Keep the codebook, an example extract for each code, dated memos on how themes were built, and a record of decisions that changed. **Write it as you go**: an audit trail rebuilt afterwards is a justification, and readers can usually tell.
notes.57: Triangulation uses more than one method, source or observer on the same question, like two bearings fixing a point. Denzin's four types are method, source, observer and theory, and most people use only the first. **Observer triangulation is cheap and rarely done.** Agreement between sources sharing a bias proves nothing.
notes.58: Picture three lines of sight on one question: observation shows what people do, interviews what it means to them, documents and data the scale. One bearing is a guess and three fix a position. Ask of your own design **which of the three you are missing**.
notes.59: Observe first, then interview. Seeing a practice lets you ask about the specific thing you watched and use the words people use. Ask without implying deceit: 'I noticed the queue formed differently on Tuesday' opens the topic, and 'you said everyone is served in order, but...' **closes it**.
notes.60: Attendance sheets, muster rolls and minutes are claims about reality, written under incentives. Observation tests them: does the attendance sheet match the children you counted? A mismatch is a finding, and **fraud is only one of several explanations**. Often a requirement simply does not match the work.
notes.61: Numbers locate a problem and observation finds the mechanism. Immunisation dipped in Q3, and the session had moved to a day women cannot attend. **Pair any surprising statistic with a visit to where it is produced.** It also works the other way, when observation yields a hypothesis for a survey to size.
notes.62: Convergence raises confidence only if the sources are independent and could have disagreed. Two observers from the same organisation with the same expectations agree for reasons unrelated to what happened. Ask what would have had to occur for the sources to differ. **If nothing plausible, their agreement tells you nothing.**
notes.63: Disagreement between sources is information. The attendance sheet says 30 and you counted 18: reporting pressure, or an unusual day? Each row has at least two readings, and only more evidence separates them. **Treat divergence as a question to investigate**, and report it, since it is harder to write than agreement.
notes.64: Pair observers who differ in gender, language, caste or familiarity, because they will notice different things. Compare notes before you discuss interpretations, so one view cannot contaminate the other. **The difference between the two sets of notes is itself data.**
notes.65: Make triangulation a habit from design onward. Plan more than one line of sight per question, record which method produced which claim, treat disagreement as a lead and report what you could not triangulate. **Triangulation attempted at write-up** asks for data you did not collect.
notes.67: Ask 'so what?' of every finding. 'Attendance is low' is a fact, and 'attendance is low on market days' points to moving the session. A finding that survives the question points at a decision. Where staff **systematically work around a rule**, the rule is usually what needs changing.
notes.68: An insight is actionable and non-obvious. Check both halves: could someone act differently, and does it change how you understand the problem? 'Attendance is low' fails both. **The mechanism turns a fact into an insight**, and observation is the method best placed to supply it.
notes.69: The funnel narrows on purpose: many observations, fewer coded patterns, fewer insights, a handful of decisions. Your job is choosing which patterns deserve action. **Resist reporting everything you saw.** Each stage should discard material and keep a trail of why.
notes.70: A recommendation says who should do what by when. 'Improve services' and 'increase community awareness' fail that test, while 'CDPO to reissue the session timing by June' passes. **Check feasibility with the person who would do it** before you write it down, and tie it to the observation behind it.
notes.71: Take findings back to frontline workers and communities, in a meeting or a page in the local language. This is member checking: it respects people and tests your reading. **Workers will tell you where you misread a routine**, a correction you cannot get any other way.
notes.72: The strongest use of observation is a routine loop of supervision visits that watch and act. Compare it with a one-off study: light and continuous where the study is deep and occasional, correcting while there is time. Without **a route for what is seen to reach someone who can change it**, it is monitoring theatre.
notes.73: State what a few sites can carry: a mechanism, a hypothesis, evidence that a practice exists. They cannot carry a district-wide claim or a prevalence estimate. Over-reach usually happens in the summary, where careful findings get compressed. **Pair with survey data for any claim about scale.**
notes.74: Lead with the insight and its so-what, add one vivid observed example, show the triangulation, and name the decision and its owner. Methodology goes in the annex. **The mother who leaves before the weighing** stays in a reader's mind longer than a completion statistic.
notes.76: You are the camera and you are biased, so the useful question is which biases are at work and what you are doing about them. Each discipline in the table reduces one source and removes none. **Report which you used and which you could not.**
notes.77: People act differently when watched. The effect peaks on the first visit and fades with time, so repeat visits help most. Keep recording minimal and name the effect in your methods. The slide adds that **the original Hawthorne evidence is weaker than the label suggests**, though the phenomenon is real.
notes.78: Attention filters what you see by what you expect. The invisible gorilla study shows people missing something obvious while they count. The last row matters most: **you cannot notice what you missed**, so a second observer is the real remedy. Also write your expectations down beforehand.
notes.79: Confirmation bias is the most dangerous bias because it feels like insight: each session the pattern looks clearer because you notice confirming cases more readily. Write your expectations down before fieldwork, then **check your notes for evidence against them**. Keep observing past the point of comfort.
notes.80: Going native is the opposite of detachment: you stop questioning the group's assumptions. Detachment feels like insufficiency and going native feels like understanding, so it is **harder to spot from inside**. Schedule someone who was not there to read your notes and ask what the setting trained you to skip.
notes.81: Reflexivity means examining how your assumptions and reactions shape what you observe, and recording it as data. Keep a journal from day one: what you expected, what irritated you, how people responded. Written at the end it is recollection; **written throughout it is evidence about how the data was produced**.
notes.82: Your gender, caste, class, age, language and agency shape what people show you. The table lists what each opens and what it closes. The last row is the practitioner's problem: **if your organisation funds the programme, people are managing an audit**. Name your position in the methods.
notes.83: No technique makes observation objective. Together they make it checkable: prolonged engagement, triangulation, disconfirming cases, low-inference notes, audit trail, member checking, reflexivity. Report which you used. **Peer debriefing is the cheapest and least used**: a colleague who was not there argues with your reading.
notes.85: Ethics runs through every minute and no form signed at the end settles it. It covers what you write as well as how you watch. The third row is the one people forget: a consented observation written so that it identifies someone in a small village **has already caused harm**.
notes.86: Consent means people know who you are, that you are observing, what you will record, where it goes and that they may decline at no cost. A gatekeeper's permission is not a person's consent: a headmaster's yes is not a child's. **Consent is continuous**, as people come and go.
notes.87: Match your duty to the setting. In public space privacy is low, but you still do not single people out. Semi-public places such as clinics and schools need institutional permission and individual consent, and **permission from the block officer is not consent from the woman in the queue**. Private spaces need explicit consent.
notes.88: Consent to be observed is not consent to be photographed, and neither is consent to publication. Get separate consent for camera and audio, and let people say yes to observation and no to the camera. Note the DPDP date and **decide storage and deletion before fieldwork**.
notes.89: The observer holds more power: literacy, backing, the ability to leave. A request from an outsider can sound like an order. Make refusal costless, ask separately from the official who brought you, and use the person's language. **If nobody ever declines in a whole study, consent was not real.**
notes.90: What you write can expose people. In a small village a few attributes identify someone with no name. Coarsen details, aggregate, store notes securely and know your referral duty before you go. For a **workaround**, report the pattern and the rule, never the person or the site.
notes.91: Covert observation needs four things at once: important knowledge, no other method, minimal harm and independent ethics approval. Most proposals fail on the second, since prolonged overt engagement would have worked. If you are hiding why you are there, **ask whether the study should happen at all**.
notes.92: Ethical observation asks what flows back. Give findings to frontline staff before the report is final, to the community in their language, and to decision-makers with an owner and a date. The test: **would the people you observed feel fairly treated** if they read what you wrote?
notes.94: Decide before you go: question, type, site and timing, tool, consent and recording. Timing is a sampling decision in disguise, since 11 a.m. on a Tuesday tells you about 11 a.m. on Tuesdays. **Visit at more than one time and day** if you want to say what is typical.
notes.95: Use one page for every session: header, sketch map, descriptive column, reflective column marked [OC], verbatim quotes and follow-ups. The last row, questions raised, **turns a set of visits into a study**, since each session starts sharper. A template that changes between sessions cannot be compared.
notes.96: Match tool to need: paper for jottings, voice memos for dictating expanded notes on the way home, KoboToolbox or ODK for offline structured counts, a spreadsheet or Taguette for coding. Dictating on the journey home is **the most effective single habit** in this deck. Tools serve the method.
notes.97: Five pitfalls, each prevented by a habit: writing up later, recording judgements, forgetting that the notebook changes behaviour, over-claiming, and skipping consent. The first is committed by everyone and noticed by nobody. **Notes written three days on feel vivid** and have reorganised around your conclusion.
notes.98: A short reading list with a clear order. If you are going to the field this month, start with Emerson, Fretz and Shaw on writing notes. Keep Spradley open during a first study and read Geertz for thick description. **Gold (1958)** gives the observer-role continuum from section 2.
notes.99: Five things to take away: watch what people do, use a framework, write up the same day, triangulate, observe ethically. The slide's table swaps the last for describing before interpreting. The third decides whether the rest matter, because **everything else operates on your notes**. If you keep one, keep the say-do gap.
